quote: The banners of the King of Hell advance
note: In the poem this line is in Latin: "Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni." The first three words open a famous hymn by Venantius Fortunatus, sung in the week before Easter: "The banners of the King advance", meaning the cross of Christ. Virgil adds one word, "of Hell", and turns it into a grim parody. The banners are Lucifer's wings.
The first sight of Lucifer: something huge, dim and mechanical, with great arms turning in the murk. The likeness prepares for what he is, a machine of wind and grinding with no sign of mind.

context: Dante speaks to no one here and names no one. The souls are sealed under the ice in every posture, and the poets walk over them.

quote: the creature who once possessed perfect beauty
context: The climax of the descent is not a terrifying prince of evil but a trapped giant who chews, weeps and flaps his wings, and never speaks or notices his visitors.

note: A Roman name for Pluto, god of the underworld. Virgil, a Roman, uses it for Lucifer. The walled city of lower Hell was also called Dis (Inferno 8), after its king.
One of the moments where Dante turns from the story to speak to the reader directly, here to admit that words cannot do what he needs.

quote: I did not die, yet I was not alive
note: A state between life and death, numb with cold and terror. It is also a fair description of Lucifer and of all the damned, who exist forever without really living.

quote: The Emperor of the sorrowful kingdom
note: The dark counterpart of God, whom Virgil called "that Emperor who reigns above" in Inferno 1. This emperor is stuck in ice to the chest and governs nothing.
The giants of Canto 31 were as tall as towers. Dante says he is closer in size to one of them than a giant is to one of Lucifer's arms.
Lucifer's revolt was the first sin, and he then tempted humanity into its own. Ingratitude toward his maker makes him the first and greatest traitor, so he sits at the center of the traitors' circle.
A hideous reversal of the Trinity, the three persons of the one God. Lucifer wanted to be like God, and he has become God's mirror image, with everything turned to its opposite.

The meaning of the three colors is disputed. The oldest reading sets them against the Power, Wisdom and Love that made Hell (Inferno 3): red for hatred, pale yellow for powerlessness, black for ignorance. Another takes them as the peoples of the three continents then known, Europe, Asia and Africa, all under his sway.
Ethiopia, the upper Nile. The left face is black.

Six wings in all. In the Book of Isaiah (6:2) the seraphim, the highest order of angels, each have six wings, and Lucifer was held to have been among the highest. He keeps the wings of his rank, but they are now a bat's, a creature of the dark.
The answer to Dante's question in Canto 33 about where the wind comes from. They are also a mockery of the Holy Spirit, which comes as a breath or wind. That wind gives life. These freeze.

context: Lucifer is his own jailer. The beating of his wings, as if to fly free, is what freezes the lake that holds him and everyone in it.

note: The king of Hell is its chief victim. He weeps from rage and pain, not remorse.

context: He has the central mouth and the worst pain: he goes in head first, and his back is flayed by the claws as well.

For Dante, God willed two powers to guide the world: the Church for the soul and the Roman Empire for earthly peace. Judas betrayed the founder of one, Brutus and Cassius the founder of the other, Julius Caesar. Brutus suffers without a sound, perhaps a trace of his fame as a Stoic.
The ancient writers describe Cassius as lean. Dante's sturdy figure may come from confusing him with another Cassius, whom Cicero calls fat.

note: The evening of Holy Saturday. The poets entered Hell at nightfall on Good Friday, so the whole descent has taken twenty-four hours.
The only way out of Hell is down Lucifer's own body, in the gap between his hairy sides and the ice. Evil itself becomes the ladder.

quote: the point where the thigh turns
note: Lucifer's hip is at the exact center of the earth, which for Dante is the center of the universe and the point toward which everything heavy falls.

quote: turned his head where his feet had been
note: At the center, down becomes up. Virgil has to turn himself right around and start climbing, with great effort, because he is now moving away from the center. Dante, not understanding, thinks they are going back.
From the far side of the center, Lucifer appears upside down, his legs sticking up into the cavern. It is the same body seen from the other hemisphere.
The center of the earth. Dante teases the reader who is as slow to work it out as he was.

The Italian is "mezza terza", halfway through the first division of the church's day, about half past seven in the morning. A few minutes ago it was nightfall. By crossing the center the poets have passed to the other side of the globe, where the time is twelve hours different, so it is Saturday morning over again.

quote: the evil worm who pierces the world
note: Lucifer sits in the earth like a worm at the core of a rotten fruit. "Worm" was also an old word for a serpent or dragon.
The sky of the southern half of the globe. In Dante's geography all the inhabited land lies in the northern half, with Jerusalem at its center, and the southern half is open ocean.

quote: the Man who was born and lived without sin
note: Christ, crucified at Jerusalem. As everywhere in Hell, he is not named. Dante is now directly underneath the opposite point of the globe.
A small round floor of rock, the reverse side of the ice of Judecca. The frozen lake is above their heads now, on the other side.

quote: On this side he fell from heaven
note: Dante's own myth of how the world got its shape. Lucifer fell head first onto the southern hemisphere. The land that was there fled under the sea and came up in the north. As he drove on to the center, the earth in his path shrank from him too.

quote: the land that appears on this side
context: The earth that fled upward from Lucifer left the cavern where the poets stand, and heaped up as the one island of the southern sea: the mountain of Purgatory. The place where souls are saved was made by Satan's fall.

note: Another name for Lucifer. In the Gospels, Beelzebub is the prince of devils.
Usually read as Hell itself, or the cavern, as Lucifer's grave. The sense is that the passage up to the surface is as long as Hell is deep.
Not named. Many commentators take it to be Lethe, the river at the top of Purgatory that washes away the memory of sin (Purgatorio 28), carrying that sin back down to Hell where it began.

A climb as long as the whole descent, told in a few lines. It takes nearly a full day: the poets come out on the shore of Purgatory shortly before dawn on Easter Sunday, the morning of the Resurrection.
The poem's most famous last line: "E quindi uscimmo a riveder le stelle." Hell has no sky. Each of the three parts of the Comedy ends on the same word, "stelle", stars.
